CMS Part B beneficiaries (HCPCS J0174): 961 in 2023 and 7,907 in 2024 (Medicare Part B Spending by Drug, dataset 76a714ad-3a2c-43ac-b76d-9dadf8f7d890) and 14,029 in 2025 (Medicare Quarterly Part B Spending by Drug, bf6a5b3b-31ee-4abb-b1ad-2607a1e7510a, '2025 (Q1-Q4)'). Stopping 17.39% a year as above, so new starts are 961, 7,907 - 961 x 0.8261 = 7,113 and 14,029 - 7,907 x 0.8261 = 7,497. Over the 2,200,000 US residents eligible for lecanemab (Dittrich A et al., Neurology 2024, doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000209402, PMC11175644) less those already started, capture is 0.0437%, 0.3235% and 0.3420%. MULTIPLE 2.0, A JUDGEMENT: 26 Leqembi infusions a year against 13 for prasinezumab, on the reading that Leqembi's flat new starts in 2024 and 2025 against a 2.2 million pool show a bound set by infusion and MRI capacity rather than by demand. 2.0 x 0.3420% = 0.684%
column12: the multiple is the most arguable figure here. For more: no ARIA and so no MRI safety schedule, no amyloid PET or CSF confirmation, and Parkinson's is managed by neurologists who already see these patients. Against: PADOVA missed its primary endpoint, early patients are functional on levodopa and may decline a monthly infusion, and Leqembi's own maintenance moved to four-weekly in 2025. Published peaks do not settle it: GlobalData's 'over $1.5B' US peak (Clinical Trials Arena, 22 February 2021) predates PADOVA and PARAISO; Roche's FTI consensus carries CHF 0.2bn of prasinezumab sales in 2030, a risk-adjusted pre-launch year. The anchor also leans low on scope: the Part B file counts Medicare fee-for-service patients only, against a pool of every eligible US resident, and trontinemab carries the same basis
